Raikva
------------------------------------------
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was the king of Mahāvṛṣa and well-known for his generosity, especially for gifting ड़ोओद् to the poor and the needy. Once he over-heard two swans flying over his palace, conversing between them. While one sang his praise, the other belittled it saying that the sage रैक्व was far superior to him.
Becoming curious about this रैक्व, the king despatched his servants in search of him. After a long search रैक्व was located in a lonely place, sitting under his cart and scratching his itches.
When the king approached him for the special knowledge in which he was an adept, offering him wealth and his own daughter in मर्रिअगे, रैक्व obliged by teaching him the Saṁvarga Vidyā.
Saṁvarga is that which absorbs other things into itself. वायु (the air or the wind) in the outside world and प्राण (the vital air, the life force) inside the human body are the saṁvargas since they, respectively, absorb into themselves the four cosmic objects (sun, मोओन्, fire and water) and the four internal organs (speech, eyes, ears and मिन्द्).
Jānaśruti also gave रैक्व, a number of villages. The whole area came to be known as Raikvaparṇa.
This story is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (

-8).
The Skandapurāṇa (Setukhaṇḍa 26) refers to a sage रैक्व, who was lame and always travelled by a bullock cart. Hence he was called ‘Sayugva-रैक्व’, the ‘Raikva with a cart pulled by two bullocks’.
He is said to have drawn to himself the three sacred rivers गङ्गा, यमुना, and गया, with the desire to bathe in them, to the place (in the गन्धमादन mountains) where he lived. They manifested themselves there as desired by him.
The two Raikvas appear to be the same.
